summary_html: Agency fails to **disclose required data or reports**, obstructing transparency. Federal statutes require public reporting under CAPTA, FOIA, and Sunshine provisions.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — mandates public availability of child-fatality information  
- **Freedom of Information Act (5 U.S.C. § 552)** — public access to federal records  
- **Government in the Sunshine Act (5 U.S.C. § 552b)** — open-meeting requirements

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Ray v. Department of Human Resources
key_cases.holding: The court reversed, holding that a juvenile court may order disclosure of otherwise confidential DHR child-abuse records when it finds disclosure necessary to resolve an issue before it, and that parental rights may not be terminated on a bare 'welfare of the child' test without a showing of parental unfitness.
key_cases.relevance: It identifies the statutory mechanism by which confidentiality of child-abuse records yields to a court's need for the information.
key_cases.quote: it is not proper to consider the question of termination of parental rights based solely upon a "welfare of the child" test, without some required showing of parental unfitness

key_cases.case_name: Southeastern Legal Foundation, Inc. v. Ledbetter
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia held that clinical records made confidential by OCGA 37-3-1(2) fall outside the Open Records Act's disclosure command, so the newspapers could not obtain a state hospital patient's mental health records under that Act.
key_cases.relevance: It identifies the statutory mechanism agencies invoke to withhold human-services records from the public.
key_cases.quote: the disclosure provisions of OCGA § 50-18-70 (b) do not apply to clinical records as defined by OCGA § 37-3-1 (2)

key_cases.case_name: Georgia Department of Human Services, Division of Family and Children Services v. Steiner
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed the superior court and upheld the central child abuse registry as applied, holding that listing as a substantiated abuser did not, on this record, satisfy the stigma-plus test and so triggered no federal procedural due process protection, and that 'some evidence' supported the ALJ's substantiation.
key_cases.relevance: It confirms that registry records and the associated administrative hearing are sealed from the general public.
key_cases.quote: Steiner failed to demonstrate a constitutionally protected liberty or property interest sufficient to trigger the due process protections that he claims were violated by operation of the registry

key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed a declaratory judgment striking down Georgia's former central child abuse registry, holding that a person classified as a confirmed abuser has more than a reputational interest at stake and that the statute's absolute bar on compelling testimony from a child under 14 denies due process in a large fraction of cases, so the entire Act, OCGA 49-5-180 et seq., had to fall.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Georgia decision holding that the confidentiality and closed-hearing architecture of the abuse registry cannot be maintained on procedures that deny the accused the ability to test the evidence.
key_cases.quote: The portion of OCGA § 49-5-183.1 that precludes an accused from compelling a child's testimony in the administrative proceedings is unconstitutional and central to the general scope of the Act

key_cases.case_name: Floyd County Grand Jury v. Department of Family & Children Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed an order quashing grand jury subpoenas to seven DFACS employees, holding that county departments of family and children services are instrumentalities of the state Department of Human Resources rather than county offices, so a grand jury has no power under OCGA 15-12-71(b)(2) or any other statute to conduct a civil investigation of DFACS.
key_cases.relevance: It shows that a disclosure or transparency demand aimed at DFACS must be addressed to the state, not the county, and cannot be compelled by county-level investigative process.
key_cases.quote: these departments are instrumentalities of the Department of Human Resources (DHR), a state agency, independent of the county, and no evidence has been presented to the contrary
